title: The start-to-run distance and running-related injury among obese novice runners: a randomized trial
authors: Bertelsen ML, Hansen M, Rasmussen S, Nielsen RO
journal: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
findings: 56 novices (BMI 30-35) were randomised to 3 km per week (3 sessions of 1 km, n=29) or 6 km per week (3 sessions of 2 km, n=27), both increasing the weekly distance by 10% per week, for 4 weeks.
Intention-to-treat cumulative risk difference for injury -16.3% (95% CI -43.8 to 11.3, p=0.25) favouring 3 km, which is not statistically significant.
Per-protocol cumulative risk difference -31.2% (95% CI -57.0 to -5.2, p=0.02); overuse-symptom risk difference -47.8% (95% CI -81.0 to -14.6, p=0.01).
Five participants ran much more than prescribed and 15 never uploaded any training, which is why a supplementary per-protocol analysis was performed.
The study hypothesised 20% fewer injuries with the 3 km start; level of evidence 2b.
limitations: Underpowered; the primary ITT result is not significant; the per-protocol analysis is supplementary and affected by non-adherence and missing data (15 of 56 uploaded nothing); only 4 weeks and only BMI 30-35; session duration and pace are not reported in the abstract.
implications: Supports a BMI-scaled first-week dose of about 3 sessions of about 1 km (roughly 3 km per week) for BMI 30 and above, as a grade C value with a note that the primary ITT test was null.
1 km at an easy novice pace is a short session (likely well under 20 min; pace is not reported), so 3 x 20 min of continuous running should not be the floor for BMI 30+ novices.
